Chippewa

Chippewa is an overlapping name used in Ojibwe language references and in the names of distinct communities and governments. This is an alternate doorway to Ojibwe reading routes, beginning with a regional dictionary, the Sault Tribe’s language account and Bois Forte’s own history.

Read the sources [3] Ojibwe People’s Dictionary; University of Minnesota American Indian Studies and University Libraries, with Ojibwe contributors [4] saulttribe.com

These photographs have individual, documented connections to this entry. Their captions and source records define the people, place, object, and period shown; no one photograph represents every community within a broader label.

Bandolier Bag, Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) artist
Saint Louis Art Museum, Gift of Elizabeth B. and Robert Wells Streett, 20:2022; Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) artist, name unrecorded

Source & image record ↗ · Public Domain, as designated by the museum; its Terms of Use explicitly permit unrestricted use of Public-domain Content. No Creative Commons license asserted.

The inspected dictionary lists Chippewa among Ojibwe language names. The existing museum record explicitly attributes this c.1860 bag to an Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) artist, individually unrecorded. Reuse as an overlapping-name Ojibwe reading illustration; do not assign it to a particular Chippewa government or make it universal to every Anishinaabe people. One Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) artist's nineteenth-century bandolier bag, c. 1860. Suitable for the broad Anishinaabe profile only with the precise Ojibwe attribution retained. Do not imply one object represents all Anishinaabe nations or governments, copy its beadwork as generated filler, or infer symbolism beyond the inspected museum record. RISD 43.119 remains an image-retrieval gap. Used one bounded museum alternative: SLAM object 20:2022. Actual museum page read, Public Domain link and Terms of Use read, image URL extracted from the official page HTML, original 1057 x 1600 JPEG downloaded and visually inspected in full. Object attribution is explicitly Anishinaabe (Ojibwe), not merely geographic. No maker biography, separate community review, or detailed design meanings established. Web copies proportionally resized/recompressed without retouching; CSS crops and overlays are presentation only. Complete image displayed proportionally in the page banner. The same precisely identified Ojibwe artist’s bag may accompany the broad Ojibwe collection as well as Anishinaabe. The maker’s individual name and particular Ojibwe government/community are unrecorded in the inspected item. It must not be assigned specifically to one Minnesota Band, used as a universal Ojibwe design, or copied into invented traditional motifs.

Start reading here

Alternate-name route sharing the broader Ojibwe collection. Chippewa, Ojibwe and Anishinaabe have overlapping but context-dependent usage, while Anishinaabe also has wider uses.

  1. Ojibwe People’s Dictionary: language, speakers and selected documentation guides

    Start with the dictionary’s name usage, regional scope and contributor methodology.

  2. Ojibwe Language - The Sault Tribe of Chippewa Indians Official Web Site

    Read a specifically attributed Sault Tribe language perspective.

  3. History — Bois Forte Band of Chippewa

    Continue with Bois Forte’s local historical account, keeping its community scope.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

An overlapping name, with local scope

The dictionary includes Chippewa among names used for Ojibwe and identifies its own Central Southwestern regional focus. Its speakers, spellings and examples should be read with those limits.

Read the sources [3] Ojibwe People’s Dictionary; University of Minnesota American Indian Studies and University Libraries, with Ojibwe contributors

02

Read community voices separately

The Sault Tribe’s language account and Bois Forte’s history come from distinct governments. They offer specific perspectives on language continuity and local historical experience rather than a single history for every community called Chippewa.

Read the sources [4] saulttribe.com [5] Bois Forte Band of Chippewa

Ojibwe People’s Dictionary: language, speakers and selected documentation guides ↗

A regionally focused dictionary collection explains spelling, speaker attribution and word-building. Selected methodology and contributor accounts were read together as one work. Historical speaker figures and undated biographical roles are not treated as current; no audio was played.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual language introduction, project history, regional key and selected English contributor accounts; word-stem and audio-method text inspected. Scope is selected text, not the complete dictionary.

Review recorded: October 21, 2026

Ojibwe Language - The Sault Tribe of Chippewa Indians Official Web Site ↗

Publication: Updated 2019-06-13

A Sault Tribe account connects Anishinaabeg language with cultural continuity, describes intergenerational language suppression and lists revitalization work. This voice is specific to one Michigan-based tribal government and is used as a wider regional perspective, not as a Minnesota Band account.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read the full Ojibwe Language page, including the dated language-program description and linked culture guidance (lines 98–107). The linked programs were not independently reviewed.

Review recorded: October 22, 2026

https://www.saulttribe.com/history-a-culture/our-culture/103-ojibwe-language

Indigenous-ledBois Forte Band of ChippewaSource 5

History — Bois Forte Band of Chippewa ↗

Publication: Undated public history page; 2026 site footer not treated as publication date

The Band distinguishes its three reservation sectors and gives its own migration account, treaty chronology and present-day resource and community context. Its account is not treated as a boundary map or as a template for other Ojibwe communities.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read the complete visible Brief Summary of Bois Forte History (lines 134–145): community locations, migration account, 1854 and 1866 treaties, 1881 executive order, self-government and cultural/resource continuity. Contemporary business totals are not repeated.

Review recorded: October 22, 2026

https://boisforte.com/about/history/
